sections.title: A painted wall older than farming
sections.intro_md:
In 1957 an archaeologist from Ujjain named **Vishnu Shridhar Wakankar** was travelling by train between Bhopal and Itarsi when he noticed a line of strange sandstone towers in the forest. By his own account they reminded him of the painted caves he had seen in Spain and France. He got off, walked in, and found walls covered in red and white figures: hunters, dancers, bison, elephants, a man being thrown by a boar.

That site was **Bhimbetka**, 45 km south of Bhopal. It now counts more than 750 rock shelters, about 400 of them painted, and people have sheltered there for over 100,000 years. UNESCO listed it in 2003.

Bhimbetka is a good way into Madhya Pradesh because the whole state works like that: an ordinary stretch of forest or plateau that turns out to hold something very old and very large. India's oldest known stone zero is in Gwalior. Ashoka's stupa is at Sanchi. The world's densest tiger forests, the last wild barasingha and the first cheetahs in India since 1952 are all here. The state sits at the centre of the country, and most of India's history has passed through it.

spotlights.name: Bhimbetka rock shelters
spotlights.when: Occupied for over 100,000 years; paintings from about 10,000 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: Red and white stick figures of hunters, horses and animals on the ceilings of giant sandstone overhangs.
spotlights.story_md: The paintings are layered like a palimpsest. The oldest, in green and dark red, are Mesolithic, from roughly 10,000 BCE; Wakankar himself argued some were far older. Later layers add horsemen, chariots and battle scenes from historic times. One shelter, nicknamed **Zoo Rock**, packs elephants, barasingha, bison and deer onto one wall. The pigments came from local minerals: haematite for red, chalk and kaolin for white, mixed with water or animal fat. They survived because the overhangs keep off rain and the rock seeps a thin mineral glaze over the paint. Wakankar spent the next three decades mapping the site.
spotlights.why_it_matters: South Asia's oldest known art, and proof that people were living in central India long before the first cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: A man looked out of a train window and saw 10,000 years of paintings.

sections.title: Madhya Pradesh at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh means 'central province', and the name is literal. It is landlocked in the middle of India, touching five states: Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and Gujarat.

It is huge: **308,252 km²**, the second-largest state after Rajasthan and bigger than Italy. Census 2011 counted **72,597,565** people, fifth in India, at 236 per km², well below the national average. Today there are **55 districts**; the last three, Mauganj, Pandhurna and Maihar, were created in 2023. The capital is **Bhopal**, the 'City of Lakes'. Indore is the biggest city and the money capital.

The state was formed on **1 November 1956** by joining Madhya Bharat, Vindhya Pradesh, Bhopal State and the Hindi-speaking part of the old Central Provinces. On 1 November 2000 it lost its south-eastern third, which became Chhattisgarh. Even after that split it remains the second-largest state.

The numbers that make it unusual are about wildness and tribes: India's largest forest area, the most tigers of any state (785 in the 2022 count), and the largest tribal population, about 1.53 crore people or 21% of the state.

spotlights.name: Bhopal's Upper Lake (Bhojtal)
spotlights.spot_it: A wide lake on Bhopal's western edge, with a statue of a king on a pillar near the shore.
spotlights.story_md: Tradition credits the Upper Lake to **Raja Bhoj** of the Paramara dynasty, who is said to have dammed the Kolans river in the 11th century to create it. It covers about 36 km² and still supplies around 40% of Bhopal's drinking water. Together with the Lower Lake it gives the city its nickname. A 2011 statue of Bhoj stands on a column at the lake's edge, and in 2011 the lake was renamed Bhojtal. On its banks rise the pink towers of the **Taj-ul-Masajid**, begun by the Begums of Bhopal and among the largest mosques in Asia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A thousand-year-old reservoir still waters a capital of two million.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king dammed a river and a city drank for a thousand years.

sections.title: The land: two ranges and a river that runs backwards
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh is mostly plateau, tilted and cut by rivers. Two long ranges run east to west across it. The **Vindhya** in the north and the **Satpura** in the south squeeze between them the valley of the **Narmada**, the state's lifeline.

North of the Vindhya lies the **Malwa plateau**, black volcanic soil from the Deccan Traps around Indore and Ujjain: cotton, soybean and wheat country. North of that, the **Chambal** has cut the land into ravines along the Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh borders. In the north-east is **Bundelkhand**, rocky and drought-prone, with the forts of Orchha and the temples of Khajuraho. In the east are the forested Maikal hills, where the Narmada and the Son both begin, near Amarkantak.

Most Indian rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal. The Narmada and the Tapti, which rises at Multai in Betul district, flow west to the Arabian Sea through rift valleys. The highest point, **Dhupgarh**, about 1,350 m, rises above the hill town of Pachmarhi in the Satpura.

spotlights.name: The Narmada

where.label: Amarkantak to the Gulf of Khambhat

spotlights.spot_it: A broad, rock-studded river flowing west, with steps and shrines at every town it touches.
spotlights.story_md: The Narmada rises at Amarkantak and runs about 1,312 km west, around 1,077 km of it inside Madhya Pradesh, before entering Gujarat and the Arabian Sea. It runs through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura, which is why it flows west against the grain of the country. Hindus treat it as so holy that a pebble from its bed, the **banalinga**, is worshipped as Shiva without being consecrated. Pilgrims walk the **Narmada Parikrama**, circling the river on foot from source to sea and back, about 2,600 km, a journey that traditionally takes three years, three months and thirteen days.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The spine of the state, its water, power and pilgrim road.
spotlights.memory_hook: The one river you walk around instead of along.

spotlights.name: Marble Rocks and Dhuandhar Falls
spotlights.spot_it: White and grey marble cliffs rising sheer from green water, best seen from a rowing boat by moonlight.
spotlights.story_md: Near Jabalpur the Narmada cuts a gorge about 3 km long through cliffs of soft magnesian limestone that look like marble, some about 30 m high. Boatmen row visitors through and recite rhyming commentary, and the rock shines white on full-moon nights. Just upstream the river drops about 30 m at **Dhuandhar**, 'the smoke cascade', named for the spray. The gorge has been used as a film location many times. Above it sits the 10th century **Chausath Yogini** temple, a circle of 64 goddess shrines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most photographed stretch of the Narmada.
spotlights.memory_hook: A river that runs between walls of marble and falls into smoke.

spotlights.name: Pachmarhi and Dhupgarh
spotlights.spot_it: Red sandstone cliffs, waterfalls and sal forest around a cantonment town, the 'Queen of Satpura'.
spotlights.story_md: In 1857 a British officer, Captain James Forsyth, rode up onto this plateau and reported a cool, well-watered hill station in the middle of hot central India. It became the summer seat of the Central Provinces. The name is often said to mean 'five caves', after the Pandava caves in the town. Around it are the **Bee Falls**, Jata Shankar and the **Dhupgarh** summit, about 1,350 m, the highest point in the state, where crowds gather for sunset. The surrounding Satpura Tiger Reserve and the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve are among the least crowded tiger forests in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Central India's only true hill station, and its highest ground.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five caves, one summit, and the coolest air between Delhi and the Deccan.

spotlights.name: The Chambal ravines
spotlights.spot_it: A maze of bare mud gullies and cliffs beside a clear river, like a miniature canyon country.
spotlights.story_md: The Chambal is one of the cleanest large rivers in India, partly because so few people have lived along it. Erosion has carved the soft soil on its banks into a belt of ravines up to about 10 km wide. For centuries the ravines made perfect hiding places, and the region became notorious for dacoits, or bandit gangs. The same emptiness saved the river's wildlife: since 1979 the **National Chambal Sanctuary**, shared by Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, protects most of the world's wild gharials, the Gangetic river dolphin and the red-crowned roof turtle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A landscape that sheltered both outlaws and endangered species.
spotlights.memory_hook: The ravines hid bandits and saved crocodiles.

sections.title: The tiger state
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh has the most tigers of any Indian state: **785** in the 2022 All India Tiger Estimation, out of a national total of about 3,682. It also has more forest by area than any other state.

There are nine tiger reserves, including **Kanha**, **Bandhavgarh**, **Pench**, **Satpura**, **Panna** and the newer Veerangana Durgavati and Ratapani reserves. Kanha is usually counted among the best-managed parks in Asia. Bandhavgarh has one of the highest densities of tigers anywhere. Panna is a comeback story: it lost all its tigers by 2009 and rebuilt a population from a few animals brought in from other parks.

The state is also where India has tried to bring back an animal it lost. The Asiatic cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952. In September 2022 eight African cheetahs flew in from Namibia to **Kuno National Park**, followed by twelve from South Africa in 2023. The project has had deaths and debate in equal measure, and it is still running.

spotlights.name: Kanha and the barasingha

where.label: Kanha Tiger Reserve, Mandla and Balaghat

spotlights.spot_it: Herds of large swamp deer with many-tined antlers grazing in open meadows ringed by sal forest.
spotlights.story_md: Kanha's meadows hold the last wild population of the hard-ground **barasingha**, a subspecies of swamp deer adapted to firm grassland. By 1970 only about 66 were left. Park managers fenced breeding enclosures, burned and restored grassland, and moved villages out; the count has since climbed to roughly 1,000. The barasingha is Madhya Pradesh's state animal, and in 2017 Kanha introduced 'Bhoorsingh the Barasingha' as the first official mascot of an Indian tiger reserve. The forests around Kanha and Pench are the country Rudyard Kipling had in mind for The Jungle Book, though he never visited.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A deer pulled back from fewer than 70 animals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixty-six deer became a thousand.

spotlights.name: Bandhavgarh
spotlights.spot_it: Tigers in bamboo and sal below a flat-topped hill crowned by a ruined fort.
spotlights.story_md: Bandhavgarh was once the hunting reserve of the Maharajas of Rewa, and its central hill carries a fort said to be some 2,000 years old, with rock-cut caves and a reclining Vishnu statue about 10 m long. The park's core has one of the highest tiger densities in India, which makes sightings common. In 2024 the deaths of about ten wild elephants in a few days, traced to toxins in kodo millet they had eaten, made national news and showed how new the elephant herds here are: they began moving in from Chhattisgarh around 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The likeliest place in India to see a wild tiger.
spotlights.memory_hook: A maharaja's hunting ground became a tiger nursery.

spotlights.name: Kuno and the cheetah return
spotlights.spot_it: Spotted cats with black tear lines on their faces, in dry grassland and open teak woodland.
spotlights.story_md: Kuno was first prepared for Asiatic lions from Gir; between 1998 and 2003 about 1,650 people, mostly Sahariya Adivasis from 24 villages, were moved out. Gujarat never sent the lions, despite a 2013 Supreme Court order. Instead, on 17 September 2022, eight cheetahs from Namibia were released into enclosures here, and twelve from South Africa arrived in February 2023. Several adults and cubs died of infections, heat and fights; but the first cubs were born on Indian soil in March 2023, and in 2025 cheetahs were also moved to Gandhi Sagar sanctuary in Mandsaur district.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's first intercontinental transfer of a large carnivore into the wild.
spotlights.memory_hook: The lions never came, so the cheetahs did.

spotlights.name: Mohan, the white tiger of Rewa
spotlights.spot_it: A tiger with white fur and chocolate stripes and blue eyes.
spotlights.story_md: In 1951 Maharaja Martand Singh of Rewa caught a white tiger cub in the forest of Bandhavgarh and named him **Mohan**. Most white tigers in zoos around the world descend from him, bred through his daughter Radha. The colour comes from a single recessive gene; such tigers are rare in the wild, and the inbreeding needed to produce them in zoos causes crossed eyes and other defects, which is why conservationists oppose it. Mohan lived until 1969. In 2016 the state opened the Maharaja Martand Singh Judev White Tiger Safari at Mukundpur, near Rewa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Nearly every white tiger you have seen in a zoo traces back to this one cub.
spotlights.memory_hook: One cub from Rewa, a white family across the world.

spotlights.name: Gharials of the Chambal
spotlights.spot_it: A slender crocodile with a long, thin snout; adult males carry a bulbous knob on the tip.
spotlights.story_md: The gharial eats fish and is no threat to people. By the mid-1970s fewer than 200 were left in the wild. The Chambal now holds the largest remaining population, by most estimates the majority of the world's wild gharials. The male's knob, the **ghara** (pot), gives the animal its name and amplifies its buzzing call. Eggs are collected from sandbanks and reared at the Deori centre near Morena before release. Sand mining in the riverbed is the chief threat today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of a species depends on one river.
spotlights.memory_hook: A crocodile named after a clay pot.

sections.title: Deep history: Narmada man, Ashoka and a Greek in Vidisha
sections.intro_md:
Central India has one of the longest human records in the subcontinent. In 1982 a geologist found a fossil skull cap in the Narmada gravels at **Hathnora**, near Hoshangabad (now Narmadapuram): still the only ancient human skull fossil found in India.

In historic times the region was **Avanti**, one of the sixteen great kingdoms of the Buddha's era, with its capital at **Ujjain**. Ujjain sat on the trade road from the Ganga plain to the western ports, and the young Ashoka governed it as viceroy. He married a merchant's daughter from Vidisha, and it was near Vidisha, at **Sanchi**, that he raised a stupa.

Later dynasties left some of India's most important early monuments here: the Shunga railings of Bharhut, now in the Indian Museum in Kolkata; the pillar of a Greek ambassador at Vidisha; and under the Guptas the cave temples of **Udayagiri**. Ujjain remained a centre of astronomy: Indian geographers long put their prime meridian through it.

spotlights.name: The Narmada skull
spotlights.spot_it: A brown fossil skull cap, the top of a head, in a display case.
spotlights.story_md: Arun Sonakia of the Geological Survey of India spotted the skull cap in Narmada river gravels at Hathnora. It was first classed as *Homo erectus*; later study suggested it is closer to archaic *Homo sapiens* or a mixed form, and its age is argued, with estimates ranging from about 50,000 to over 200,000 years. Later digs at the site found a collarbone and ribs that may be from other individuals. It remains the only hominin skull fossil found in India, which is why the find still matters so much.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's single fossil window into who lived here before modern humans.
spotlights.memory_hook: All of India's ancient human skulls fit in one hand: this one.

spotlights.name: The Great Stupa at Sanchi
spotlights.spot_it: A low hemispherical dome on a hilltop with four elaborately carved stone gateways at the compass points.
spotlights.story_md: Ashoka built the first brick stupa here in the 3rd century BCE. A century later it was doubled in size and faced with stone, and in the 1st century BCE the four **toranas**, or gateways, were added. They are carved like ivory: the jatakas, the Buddha's life and great processions. But the Buddha himself never appears as a human figure. He is shown only by symbols: an empty throne, a footprint, a tree, a wheel. Sanchi was abandoned and forgotten until a British officer, General Henry Taylor, recorded it in 1818. UNESCO listed it in 1989.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Among the oldest stone structures in India and the best place to see early Buddhist art.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Buddha shown everywhere by being nowhere.

spotlights.name: The Heliodorus pillar
spotlights.spot_it: A plain stone column with a bell-shaped top, locally called Khamb Baba and worshipped with vermilion.
spotlights.story_md: Its inscription says it was set up by **Heliodorus, son of Dion**, an ambassador from the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas of Taxila, who calls himself a devotee of Vasudeva, a form of Vishnu-Krishna. It is one of the earliest known records of Krishna worship and of a foreigner adopting an Indian faith. Another line on it gives a moral rule that could sit in the Mahabharata: three steps to immortality, self-restraint, charity and vigilance. Excavations around it found the foundations of an even older temple.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a Greek diplomat followed Krishna in the 2nd century BCE.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Greek named Sun-gift worshipped Krishna in Vidisha.

spotlights.name: Udayagiri caves and the Varaha
spotlights.spot_it: A giant rock-cut boar-headed god lifting the earth goddess out of a sea of carved figures.
spotlights.story_md: Twenty rock-cut shrines at Udayagiri date to the reign of Gupta king **Chandragupta II**, with inscriptions from around 401 CE. Cave 5 holds the masterpiece: Vishnu as **Varaha**, a man's body with a boar's head, about 4 m tall, lifting the earth goddess Bhudevi from the ocean while rows of gods and sages watch. Many historians read it as political art: the king as rescuer of the land. It is among the earliest large Hindu sculptures that survive in place.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Gupta age, when classical Hindu art took shape, carved on one hillside.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boar the size of a wall rescuing the world.

sections.title: Temples, forts and the first zero
sections.intro_md:
Between the 9th and 16th centuries central India was divided among strong regional dynasties, and each built in stone.

The **Gurjara-Pratiharas** held Gwalior, where a small rock-cut temple carries the oldest known stone inscription of zero as a written digit. The **Paramaras** ruled Malwa from Dhar and Ujjain; their most famous king, **Bhoja**, was a poet, patron and builder whose name is everywhere in the state. The **Chandelas** of Bundelkhand built Khajuraho. The **Kachchhapaghatas** and later the **Tomars** held Gwalior Fort.

From 1401 Malwa was an independent sultanate with its capital at **Mandu**, a fortified plateau of palaces and water tanks. The Mughals took it in 1561. In the 16th and 17th centuries the **Bundela** Rajputs built Orchha on an island in the Betwa, and the Gond kingdoms held the forests of Mandla and Garha in the south-east.

spotlights.name: Khajuraho
spotlights.spot_it: Sandstone temples rising in clustered peaks like a mountain range, every surface covered in carved figures.
spotlights.story_md: The Chandela kings built about 85 temples here; about 25 survive, Hindu and Jain side by side. The tallest, **Kandariya Mahadeva**, rises about 31 m and carries more than 800 sculptures. Khajuraho is famous for its erotic carvings, but they make up a small share, around 10% of the sculpture: most show gods, dancers, musicians, warriors and daily life. Remote and unvisited for centuries, the temples escaped destruction. A British surveyor, T. S. Burt, was guided to them in 1838. UNESCO listed them in 1986.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The high point of north Indian temple architecture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight hundred figures on one temple, and only a few are doing what everyone talks about.

spotlights.name: The zero at Chaturbhuj temple
spotlights.spot_it: A small rock-cut shrine on the fort's eastern slope, with an inscription panel beside the door.
spotlights.story_md: In 876 CE a man named Alla, a Pratihara official, recorded a gift to this Vishnu shrine: a garden measuring 187 by 270 hastas, and a daily supply of 50 garlands of flowers. In '270' and '50' the final digit is a small circle. That makes it the earliest known stone inscription of zero written as a round digit in a place-value system, the ancestor of the 0 on every keyboard. The Bakhshali manuscript has older zeros on birch bark, but nothing carved in stone is older.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where the number zero is first set in stone, in the form we still use.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty garlands a day gave the world its oldest stone zero.

spotlights.name: Bhojeshwar temple, Bhojpur
spotlights.spot_it: A plain square shrine without a tower, holding one of the largest Shiva lingas in India.
spotlights.story_md: Raja Bhoja began this temple in the 11th century and never finished it. The linga is about 2.3 m tall on a platform about 6.6 m square, carved from a single block. Because work stopped mid-way, the site shows how such temples were built: a huge earthen ramp for hauling stone still survives, and architectural drawings are engraved on the rocks around it. Nobody knows why it was abandoned. Theories include war, a structural failure of the dome, or Bhoja's death.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A building site frozen for nine hundred years.
spotlights.memory_hook: The temple stopped, so we can see how temples started.

spotlights.name: Gwalior Fort
spotlights.when: Walls from 8th century; Man Mandir palace about 1500
spotlights.spot_it: A sandstone wall 3 km long on a cliff, with a palace face covered in blue and yellow tiles of ducks, elephants and banana trees.
spotlights.story_md: The Mughal emperor Babur called it 'the pearl amongst the fortresses of Hind'. The cliff plateau holds a thousand years of building: the 8th century **Teli ka Mandir**, about 30 m tall; the 11th century Sas-Bahu temples; giant Jain figures cut into the rock face; and **Man Mandir**, the palace of Raja Man Singh Tomar, built around 1500, with glazed tile panels on its outer walls. The Mughals used the fort as a prison. Later Scindias held it, and it was fought over in 1858.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The fort that every power in north India wanted.
spotlights.memory_hook: A palace that wears tiles of blue ducks on a cliff.

spotlights.name: Mandu, the city of joy
spotlights.spot_it: A long arcaded palace between two lakes, and a pavilion on a cliff edge looking over the Narmada plain.
spotlights.story_md: Mandu sits on a plateau with a 37 km wall. Its sultans built the **Jahaz Mahal**, the 'ship palace', so called because between two lakes it seems to float. They also built the marble tomb of Hoshang Shah, which Shah Jahan's architects are said to have studied before the Taj Mahal. Mandu's best-known story is of **Baz Bahadur**, its last sultan, a musician, and **Rupmati**, a singer. When Akbar's general Adham Khan took the city in 1561, legend says Rupmati poisoned herself. Her pavilion faces south so she could see the Narmada.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Afghan architecture at its most romantic.
spotlights.memory_hook: A palace that floats and a queen who looked for her river.

spotlights.name: Orchha
spotlights.spot_it: A row of tall memorial towers on the bank of the Betwa, reflected in the water at sunset.
spotlights.story_md: The Bundela Rajputs founded Orchha in 1531 on an island in the Betwa. Its best-known building, the **Jahangir Mahal**, was put up by Raja Bir Singh Deo for a single visit by his ally, the emperor Jahangir. Along the river stand 14 **chhatris**, cenotaphs of the Bundela kings, where vultures still nest. Orchha's Ram Raja temple is the only one where Rama is worshipped as a king, and police still give him a daily guard of honour. The town has fewer than 15,000 people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A whole medieval capital that the modern world mostly passed by.
spotlights.memory_hook: A palace built for a guest who came once.

spotlights.name: Chausath Yogini temple, Mitaoli
spotlights.spot_it: A circular hilltop temple with 64 small cells around an open courtyard and a central shrine.
spotlights.story_md: This round temple was built for the 64 yoginis, female deities of tantric worship, by the Kachchhapaghata kings. It has a diameter of about 52 m, and its 64 cells once held one image each. It is often said that the round shape of the old Parliament House in New Delhi, designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, was copied from it. There is no documentary evidence for that, and the story should be treated as a popular legend. The resemblance, though, is striking.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare round temple in a land of square ones.
spotlights.memory_hook: A circle of 64 goddesses, mistaken for a model of Parliament.

sections.title: Queens, Marathas and 1857
sections.intro_md:
In the 18th century the Marathas pushed north into central India, and three of their families carved out states that lasted until 1947: the **Holkars** of Indore, the **Scindias** of Gwalior and the **Pawars** of Dhar and Dewas.

Two of the most remarkable rulers in Indian history governed here, both women. **Ahilyabai Holkar** ran Indore from Maheshwar for 28 years. And the small Muslim state of **Bhopal** was ruled for more than a century by four women in succession, the Begums.

The British took control after the Anglo-Maratha wars and ran the region through the Central India Agency, a patchwork of over 100 princely states. In 1857 central India became one of the main theatres of the rebellion. Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi and Tatya Tope took Gwalior from the Scindia ruler in June 1858; the British recaptured it within days, and the Rani was killed fighting at Kotah-ki-Serai on 18 June.

spotlights.name: Ahilyabai Holkar
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in plain white holding a Shiva linga in her palm, the way she is shown in nearly every statue.
spotlights.story_md: Born to a village headman's family in Maharashtra, Ahilyabai married into the Holkars. After the deaths of her husband, father-in-law and son, she took over the state herself and ruled from **Maheshwar** on the Narmada. She was known for hearing petitions daily and for building on an all-India scale: she rebuilt the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi in 1780, and funded ghats, wells and rest houses from Kedarnath to Rameswaram. She also brought weavers to Maheshwar, starting the sari tradition there. Her 300th birth anniversary on 31 May 2025 was marked across the state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the most admired rulers of 18th century India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The queen who held a linga and rebuilt Kashi.

spotlights.name: The Begums of Bhopal
spotlights.spot_it: Formal portraits of veiled women in jewels and medals, one of them in a full burqa with eye slits.
spotlights.story_md: From 1819 to 1926 Bhopal was ruled by four women: Qudsia Begum, her daughter Sikandar Begum, granddaughter Shah Jahan Begum, and great-granddaughter Sultan Jahan Begum. They built railways, a postal system, a modern police force and waterworks. Sikandar Begum was one of the first Indian rulers to make the Hajj. Sultan Jahan Begum was the first chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University and ran Bhopal while wearing a burqa. Shah Jahan Begum began the Taj-ul-Masajid. No other Indian state had a century of women rulers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A century of women's rule in a princely state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four generations, one throne, no kings.

spotlights.name: Rani Lakshmibai's last stand
spotlights.spot_it: A bronze statue of a woman on a rearing horse, sword raised, in Gwalior.
spotlights.story_md: After the British stormed Jhansi in April 1858, Lakshmibai escaped and joined Tatya Tope and Rao Sahib. On 1 June they took Gwalior when much of Scindia's army went over to them. Hugh Rose's force came back within three weeks. On 18 June the Rani, dressed as a cavalry leader, was killed in the fighting near Kotah-ki-Serai. Her samadhi is in Gwalior's Phool Bagh. Rose later wrote that she was the most dangerous of the rebel leaders.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous figure of 1857 died on Madhya Pradesh soil.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jhansi was her kingdom; Gwalior was her grave.

spotlights.name: Tatya Tope
spotlights.spot_it: A 19th century portrait of a man in a turban with a full moustache and beard.
spotlights.story_md: Tatya Tope was a Maratha general of Nana Saheb. After Gwalior fell he waged a guerrilla war across central India for ten months, crossing the Narmada and doubling back while several British columns chased him. He was betrayed by an ally, Man Singh of Narwar, captured in his sleep, tried and hanged at **Shivpuri** on 18 April 1859. A memorial stands at the spot. Some family members later claimed he escaped and someone else was hanged; most historians reject this.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The last major rebel commander of 1857.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten months on the run across the heart of India.

spotlights.name: Jai Vilas Palace, Gwalior
spotlights.spot_it: A long white European-style palace, part Italian, part Tuscan, with Corinthian columns.
spotlights.story_md: Jayajirao Scindia had this palace built in 1874 to receive the Prince of Wales. Its Durbar Hall holds two of the largest chandeliers in the world, each said to weigh about 3.5 tonnes. Before hanging them, the story goes, the architect had eight elephants hauled onto the roof to test whether it would take the weight. A silver model train once ran around the dining table carrying brandy and cigars to the guests. Much of the palace is now the Jiwajirao Scindia Museum; the family still lives in part of it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Raj-era princely palace at its most theatrical.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight elephants on the roof to test two lamps.

sections.title: The making of Madhya Pradesh, and the night of 1984
sections.intro_md:
Independent India first grouped the region into four units: **Madhya Bharat** (the old Gwalior, Indore and Malwa states), **Vindhya Pradesh** (Rewa and Bundelkhand), **Bhopal State** and the Hindi part of the **Central Provinces and Berar**. On 1 November 1956 the States Reorganisation Act merged them. Bhopal won the capital over Gwalior, Indore and Jabalpur, partly because it was central and had government buildings ready.

The new state was poor, rural and under-served. Its first decades brought big dams on the Narmada, the Bhilai steel plant (now in Chhattisgarh) and the Chambal dacoit problem, which ended with mass surrenders in the 1970s.

Then, in December 1984, Bhopal became the site of the world's worst industrial disaster. Sixteen years later, on 1 November 2000, the eastern districts became **Chhattisgarh**, taking much of the coal, iron and tribal forest with them.

spotlights.name: The Bhopal gas disaster
spotlights.spot_it: A rusting pesticide plant behind walls in old Bhopal, and a statue of a mother clutching a child.
spotlights.story_md: Shortly after midnight, water entered tank E610 at the Union Carbide pesticide plant and set off a runaway reaction. About 30 to 40 tonnes of **methyl isocyanate** gas escaped within two hours and drifted over sleeping neighbourhoods. The official immediate death toll was 2,259; the state government later confirmed 3,787 gas-related deaths, and other estimates run to 8,000 in the first weeks and more than 16,000 over time. A 2006 government affidavit counted 558,125 injuries. In 1989 Union Carbide paid a settlement of US$470 million. Its chairman, Warren Anderson, left India days after arrest and never stood trial.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's worst industrial disaster, and still a lesson in corporate and state accountability.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty tonnes of gas, one night, and a city still counting.

spotlights.name: The dacoits of Chambal
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of men in dhotis with rifles and bandoliers, posing in ravines.
spotlights.story_md: For decades the Chambal ravines sheltered gangs called **baaghi**, 'rebels', as they preferred to be known. The most famous, **Paan Singh Tomar**, was an army steeplechase runner who won national titles and went to the 1958 Asian Games, then turned outlaw over a land dispute; he was killed by police in 1981. In April 1972 several hundred dacoits, led by Madho Singh and Mohar Singh, surrendered at Joura in Morena before Jayaprakash Narayan, in a ceremony inspired by Gandhian ideas. The 2012 film Paan Singh Tomar made his story famous again.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how geography and land disputes shaped crime in central India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A national champion runner who ended up running from the police.

sections.title: People and languages: India's tribal heartland
sections.intro_md:
Hindi is the official language and the main tongue in the cities, but it shades into regional languages that change every couple of hundred kilometres. **Malvi** is spoken around Indore and Ujjain, **Nimadi** along the lower Narmada, **Bundeli** in the north-east around Sagar and Chhatarpur, and **Bagheli** in Rewa. Many speakers report all of these as 'Hindi' in the census.

The bigger story is the tribes. Madhya Pradesh has India's largest tribal population: about 1.53 crore people in 2011, 21.1% of the state. The **Bhils** of the west (Jhabua, Alirajpur, Dhar) and the **Gonds** of the south and east are the two biggest, each numbering several million. Smaller groups include the **Baiga**, **Bharia** and **Sahariya**, three of the government's 'particularly vulnerable tribal groups'. Bhili and Gondi, their languages, are each spoken by millions.

Their art, their festivals and their land rights shape the state far more than most outsiders realise.

visual.title: Where the regional languages are spoken

spotlights.name: The Bhils
spotlights.spot_it: Women in bright skirts and heavy silver jewellery; men with bows, turbans and dhol drums at a weekly haat.
spotlights.story_md: The Bhils are among the largest tribal groups in India, and Madhya Pradesh has more of them than any other state. The name is often traced to the Dravidian word for bow, **billu**, and archery still runs through their stories: in the Mahabharata the Bhil boy Eklavya cuts off his thumb for Drona. Bhil villages are scattered homesteads on hilltops, each family on its own fields, rather than clustered settlements. Their **Pithora** paintings of horses and gods on house walls and the Bhagoria festival before Holi are their best-known traditions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest tribal community in the state, with its own art and festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: The people of the bow.

spotlights.name: The Gonds
spotlights.spot_it: Village houses with painted walls, women in green or red saris with tattoos, and big group dances.
spotlights.story_md: The Gonds are among the largest Adivasi peoples in India, spread over central India, and once ruled kingdoms of their own: Garha-Mandla, Deogarh, Chanda and Kherla. The state's Gondwana name for the region, and even the geologists' 'Gondwana' supercontinent, come from them; the geologist Eduard Suess borrowed it in the 1880s from rock formations in Gond country. Gondi is a Dravidian language, related to Telugu, spoken by about 3 million people in India. Their painting tradition became famous worldwide as Gond art.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A people who gave their name to a supercontinent.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gondwana: named after the Gonds, 300 million years after the fact.

spotlights.name: The Baiga
spotlights.spot_it: Women with dense geometric tattoos on the face, back and legs; men with long hair tied in a knot.
spotlights.story_md: The Baiga live in the Maikal hills of Mandla, Dindori and Balaghat. They traditionally practised **bewar**, shifting cultivation, and refused to plough because they would not 'scratch the breast of mother earth'. Their healers are famous for knowledge of forest plants. Baiga women's **godna** tattoos cover much of the body and are done in stages from childhood to marriage. The anthropologist Verrier Elwin lived among them and wrote a book about them in 1939. Many Baiga were moved out of Kanha's core area.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the oldest forest peoples of central India.
spotlights.memory_hook: They would not plough, because the earth is a mother.

sections.title: Faith: a jyotirlinga, an island, a king who is a god
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh holds two of Hinduism's twelve **jyotirlingas**, the most sacred Shiva shrines: **Mahakaleshwar** in Ujjain and **Omkareshwar** on a Narmada island. Ujjain is also one of the four cities that host the **Kumbh Mela**, called Simhastha here, held every 12 years when Jupiter is in Leo.

The state is equally important to Buddhists, because of Sanchi, and to Jains, who form a small but old and wealthy community. There are Jain hill shrines at Sonagiri, Muktagiri and Bawangaja, and Jain temples sit beside Hindu ones at Khajuraho and Gwalior. Bhopal was a Muslim-ruled state for over two centuries and has some of India's largest mosques.

A few practices here are found nowhere else: Rama worshipped as a reigning king at Orchha, the dawn ash ritual at Mahakal, and the Narmada itself treated as a goddess you circle on foot.

spotlights.name: Mahakaleshwar, Ujjain
spotlights.spot_it: A tiered temple tower by a tank, and crowds queuing before dawn for the ash ritual.
spotlights.story_md: Mahakaleshwar is the only jyotirlinga that faces south, the direction of Yama, god of death, which is why Shiva here is Mahakala, 'lord of time and death'. Its best-known ritual is the **bhasma aarti** at about 4 am, when the linga is smeared with ash. The temple was sacked by Iltutmish in 1234 and rebuilt in the 18th century under the Scindias' minister Ranoji Shinde. In October 2022 the **Mahakal Lok** corridor opened around it, and visitor numbers rose to crores a year. Ujjain is preparing for Simhastha in 2028.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of Hinduism's twelve holiest Shiva shrines.
spotlights.memory_hook: The god who faces death, dusted in ash before sunrise.

spotlights.name: Omkareshwar and the Statue of Oneness
spotlights.spot_it: A temple-covered island in the Narmada, and on a hilltop a giant statue of a boy monk with a staff.
spotlights.story_md: The island of Mandhata is said to be shaped like the sacred syllable **Om**, hence the name. Its jyotirlinga is one of the twelve. Tradition says that here the young **Adi Shankaracharya** met his guru Govindapada. In 2023 the state unveiled the **Statue of Oneness**, a 108 ft (about 33 m) metal figure of Shankara as a 12-year-old, at the island's summit. Downstream, the Omkareshwar and Indira Sagar dams have changed the river; the Indira Sagar reservoir is among the largest in India by volume.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A pilgrimage island that combines a jyotirlinga with the newest giant statue in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: An island shaped like Om, guarded by a boy monk 108 feet tall.

spotlights.name: Ram Raja of Orchha
spotlights.spot_it: A pink and white palace-temple where armed police present arms to the deity every day.
spotlights.story_md: Legend says Queen Ganesh Kunwari brought an image of Rama from Ayodhya and placed it in her palace while a grand temple was built. When the temple was ready the image would not move, so the palace became the temple. Here Rama is not worshipped as a god alone but as **Raja**, the reigning king of Orchha. He receives a daily guard of honour from Madhya Pradesh police, a custom unique in India. Devotees offer him food, not as prasad in the usual way, but as a royal meal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living tradition of divine kingship.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only place where a god gets a police salute.

spotlights.name: Bawangaja, the 84-foot Jain
spotlights.spot_it: A colossal standing naked figure carved directly into a hillside, arms straight down.
spotlights.story_md: On a hill in the Satpura near Barwani stands a rock-cut image of **Rishabhanatha**, the first Jain tirthankara, about 84 ft (25.6 m) tall. The name Bawangaja means '52 yards', an old exaggeration of its height. It is among the tallest rock-cut Jain statues in the world, larger than the Gommateshwara at Shravanabelagola, though less famous. It stands in the meditative pose called kayotsarga. Jain pilgrims climb to it on the Kartik full moon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Evidence of a deep Jain heritage in western Madhya Pradesh.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-two yards was a stretch, but 84 feet is still huge.

sections.title: Music: Tansen's city and the Maihar school
sections.intro_md:
Hindustani classical music has deep roots in Madhya Pradesh. **Gwalior** was the court of Raja Man Singh Tomar, who championed the **dhrupad** style around 1500, and the home of **Tansen**, the greatest musician of Akbar's court. The **Gwalior gharana**, the oldest school of the later **khayal** style, grew here in the 19th century.

In the 20th century the small town of **Maihar** became a centre of instrumental music through one teacher, Allauddin Khan, whose students included Ravi Shankar and Ali Akbar Khan. Film music has deep roots here too: **Lata Mangeshkar** was born in Indore and **Kishore Kumar** in Khandwa.

The state's modern arts centre is **Bharat Bhavan** in Bhopal, opened in 1982 and designed by Charles Correa, where tribal and folk artists exhibit alongside modernists.

spotlights.name: Tansen
spotlights.spot_it: A domed Mughal tomb in a garden in Gwalior, with a small tamarind tree nearby.
spotlights.story_md: Tansen trained in Gwalior and at Vrindavan, served the Rewa court, and in 1562 was summoned by Akbar, becoming one of the **Navaratnas**, the nine jewels of his court. Legends credit him with lighting lamps by singing raga Deepak and calling rain with raga Megh Malhar; these are stories, not history. What is real is his influence on dhrupad and the ragas named after him, like Miyan ki Malhar and Darbari Kanada. He is buried in Gwalior near his Sufi teacher, Muhammad Ghaus. The **Tansen Samaroh**, held at the tomb every December, is one of India's oldest music festivals, running since 1924.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The founding name of Hindustani classical music.
spotlights.memory_hook: Singers chew the leaves of the tamarind at his tomb for a sweeter voice.

spotlights.name: Allauddin Khan and the Maihar gharana
spotlights.spot_it: A thin old man with a white beard at a sarod, in black and white photographs.
spotlights.story_md: Allauddin Khan ran away from home in Bengal as a boy to learn music, mastered dozens of instruments, and became court musician to the Maharaja of Maihar in 1918. There he built a school out of what he knew. His students became the core of 20th century Indian instrumental music: his son **Ali Akbar Khan** (sarod), his daughter **Annapurna Devi** (surbahar), and his son-in-law **Ravi Shankar** (sitar), who took Indian music to the Beatles and Woodstock. He also formed the Maihar Band, an orchestra of orphans playing instruments he invented.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Through Ravi Shankar, this small-town teacher reached the whole world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Maihar teacher, a sitar at Woodstock.

spotlights.name: Lata Mangeshkar
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a white sari with a long plait, singing with closed eyes.
spotlights.story_md: India's best-known playback singer was born in Indore to the musician and actor Deenanath Mangeshkar. Over seven decades she recorded songs in more than 30 languages; claims of her total range from 25,000 to over 30,000 songs and are not settled. She received the Bharat Ratna in 2001. Madhya Pradesh gives a national Lata Mangeshkar award for light music, started in 1984. Indore has a music academy and a museum project in her name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The voice of Hindi film music for half a century began in Indore.
spotlights.memory_hook: Indore's daughter sang for every heroine in India.

spotlights.name: Kishore Kumar
spotlights.spot_it: A man pulling a funny face at a microphone, or yodelling.
spotlights.story_md: Born Abhas Kumar Ganguly in **Khandwa**, Kishore Kumar became the most loved male playback singer of the 1970s, and an anarchic actor and director. He never trained in classical music and invented his trademark yodel from listening to records by Jimmie Rodgers and Tex Morton. He always wanted to return to Khandwa and asked to be cremated there, which he was in 1987. Fans still gather at his memorial on his birthday, 4 August, and offer doodh-jalebi, his favourite.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small-town voice that defined an era of Hindi film.
spotlights.memory_hook: Khandwa gave the world its yodel, and gets jalebi in return.

spotlights.name: Bharat Bhavan
spotlights.spot_it: Low terraces of stone stepping down a hillside to the Upper Lake, with open courtyards.
spotlights.story_md: Charles Correa designed Bharat Bhavan to sink into the hill rather than sit on it, so the buildings read as terraces and courtyards stepping down to the lake. Opened in 1982, it houses galleries, a theatre repertory, a library of poetry and an open-air amphitheatre. Its first director, J. Swaminathan, insisted on showing tribal artists as contemporary artists, not as crafts. That is how the Gond painter **Jangarh Singh Shyam** was discovered and shown here. It remains one of India's most important public arts centres.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where Indian tribal art first entered the modern art world on equal terms.
spotlights.memory_hook: An arts centre hidden in a hill.

sections.title: Crafts and textiles: sheer saris and painted forests
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh produces two of India's best-known handloom saris, and both come from small towns. **Chanderi** in Ashoknagar district weaves fabric so sheer it was compared to the 'skin of an onion'. **Maheshwar** on the Narmada weaves the reversible Maheshwari, a tradition revived after 1979.

In Bagh, a village in Dhar district, a family of Khatri printers have kept alive a hand block-printing method using river water and natural dyes.

The most famous art from the state in the last 40 years is tribal painting. **Gond art**, dots and dashes filling animal and tree shapes, and **Bhil art**, built from coloured dots, went from village walls to galleries in Paris and London. Both traditions now have Padma Shri winners.

Chanderi saris, Maheshwari saris, Bagh prints, Gond paintings and the leather toys of Indore all hold Geographical Indication tags, which protect the names.

visual.title: Two famous saris side by side

spotlights.name: Chanderi
spotlights.when: Weaving recorded since at least the 13th century; GI 2005
spotlights.spot_it: A translucent sari with a sheen, small gold butis (motifs) and a narrow zari border.
spotlights.story_md: Chanderi weavers use fine silk and cotton yarn, often silk in the warp and cotton in the weft, which gives a light, sheer cloth with a glossy face. Gold and silver zari motifs are woven in by hand with small needles, one butti at a time. The town was a Malwa stronghold and its weaving flourished under the Scindias, whose court ordered turbans and saris. Thousands of looms still work in the town today, most of them in weavers' homes. The Chanderi sari received a GI tag in 2005.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's finest handloom traditions.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cloth so thin it was compared to an onion skin.

spotlights.name: Maheshwari
spotlights.spot_it: A cotton or silk-cotton sari with a reversible border, often striped or checked, in jewel colours.
spotlights.story_md: Ahilyabai Holkar brought weavers from Surat and Mandu to Maheshwar in the 1760s, and tradition says the first designs copied the patterns on the fort's walls and niches. The key feature is the **bugdi** border, which can be worn either way. By the 1970s the craft was nearly gone. In 1979 Richard and Sally Holkar, descendants of the royal family, set up the Rehwa Society to revive it, and today the town has hundreds of looms. It is a favourite of designers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A queen's royal craft brought back by her descendants.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sari with no wrong side.

spotlights.name: Bagh print
spotlights.spot_it: Red and black geometric and floral block prints on white cotton, crisp edged.
spotlights.story_md: Bagh printing uses carved teak blocks, alum and iron mordants, and natural dyes from alizarin and iron rust. The cloth is washed repeatedly in the flowing water of the Baghini river, which printers say gives the colours their brightness. The craft was moved to Bagh by the Khatri family in the 1960s. Its master printer **Ismail Sulemanji Khatri** and his sons won national awards. Bagh prints carry a GI tag from 2008.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Natural dye block printing kept alive by one family.
spotlights.memory_hook: A river that does part of the printing.

spotlights.name: Gond painting and Jangarh Singh Shyam
spotlights.spot_it: Animals and trees filled with tiny dots, dashes and fishscale lines in bright colours on a plain ground.
spotlights.story_md: Gond people traditionally painted walls and floors with clay and colour. In 1981 J. Swaminathan's scouts for Bharat Bhavan found **Jangarh Singh Shyam**, a teenager from Patangarh, painting on village walls, and brought him to Bhopal. He moved to paper and canvas, invented much of the modern style and was shown at the Pompidou Centre in Paris in 1989. He died in Japan in 2001, aged about 39. His followers, the **Jangarh Kalam**, built a global market, and Gond painters such as Bhajju Shyam and Durga Bai Vyam received the Padma Shri.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Turned a village wall tradition into contemporary art.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boy from Patangarh hung in Paris.

spotlights.name: Bhil art and Bhuri Bai
spotlights.spot_it: Pictures made entirely of coloured dots, like grains of maize, showing village life, gods and trees.
spotlights.story_md: Traditional Bhil painting on walls includes the **Pithora** ritual murals with their horses. **Bhuri Bai**, from Pitol in Jhabua, was a construction labourer at Bharat Bhavan in the 1980s when J. Swaminathan asked her to paint. She became the first Bhil woman to paint on paper. Her style is built from dots, each said to stand for a grain of maize, and depicts village festivals, animals and trees. She received the Padma Shri in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Showed that Bhil art is as distinctive as Gond.
spotlights.memory_hook: From carrying bricks at Bharat Bhavan to hanging on its walls.

sections.title: Food: poha at dawn, Sarafa at midnight
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh eats differently in each region. **Malwa** around Indore loves snacks: poha, sev, kachori, and the city's fried and sugary night market. **Bundelkhand** and the Chambal eat robust wheat and millet. **Bhopal** carries a Mughlai, Afghan-influenced food culture from the Nawabs: kormas, kebabs and the slow-cooked **Bhopali gosht**. The tribal west eats maize roti and the black-feathered Kadaknath chicken.

Because the state grows so much wheat and soybean, wheat dishes like the steamed and baked **bafla** are everyday food, and Sehore's **Sharbati wheat** is sold across India as premium atta.

The most important food fact, though, is about Indore: it is probably the only Indian city where you can eat street food through the night, legally, by tradition. At 10 pm the jewellers of Sarafa Bazaar close their shutters and the food stalls take over the street until 2 am or later.

spotlights.name: Indori poha and jalebi
spotlights.spot_it: Yellow flattened rice topped with sev, raw onion, pomegranate and a sprinkle of jeeravan, beside hot jalebi.
spotlights.story_md: Indore's poha is steamed rather than fried, with sugar, lemon and fennel, and finished with a heap of **sev** and the city's own spice blend, **jeeravan**. It is eaten with jalebi, a sweet-and-salty pairing that seems strange to outsiders and normal to Indoris. One common account says poha came to Indore after independence with a Maharashtrian family who set up a shop near the Rajwada. Stalls start serving before 7 am, and by mid-morning the city has moved on to kachori and samosa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The breakfast that defines a city.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Indore, breakfast has a sev topping and a jalebi chaser.

spotlights.name: Sarafa Bazaar
spotlights.when: Night market for over a century
spotlights.spot_it: A jewellers' lane with shutters down and food stalls lit up, crowds at midnight.
spotlights.story_md: By day Sarafa is a bullion and jewellery market. When the shops close at about 9 to 10 pm, food vendors set up in front of them and stay until 2 or 3 am. Favourites include **bhutte ka kees**, garadu (fried yam with spices, a winter dish), sabudana khichdi, malpua, and the enormous **jalebi** called jaleba. The arrangement is old: the jewellers like the crowds because they keep the lane busy at night, which deters theft. The city has carefully rebuilt the market during smart-city works rather than shut it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's best-known night food market.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold by day, garadu by night.

spotlights.name: Dal bafla
spotlights.spot_it: Round wheat balls broken open and drowned in ghee, with dal, kadhi and chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Bafla is a cousin of Rajasthan's **baati**: wheat dough balls, but first boiled in water and then baked or roasted, which makes them softer inside. They are cracked and dunked in ghee and eaten with thin dal, green chutney and sometimes laddoos. In Malwa it is the meal for weddings, festivals and big family gatherings, and a dinner where guests compete to eat more. The boiling step is what separates Malwa's bafla from Rajasthani baati.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The signature heavy meal of the Malwa plateau.
spotlights.memory_hook: Boil it, bake it, drown it in ghee.

spotlights.name: Kadaknath
spotlights.spot_it: A chicken that is black all over: feathers, skin, beak, flesh and even the inner organs.
spotlights.story_md: The Kadaknath is a breed raised by Bhil and Bhilala families in Jhabua and Alirajpur. Its black colour comes from melanin deposited throughout the body, a trait called fibromelanosis. Locals call it **kali masi**. The meat is said to be lower in fat and higher in protein than ordinary chicken; it sells for several times the price. After a dispute with Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh won the GI tag for Jhabua's Kadaknath in 2018. Government hatcheries now supply chicks to tribal households as a source of cash income.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tribal breed that became a premium brand.
spotlights.memory_hook: A black chicken, black to the bone.

sections.title: Festivals: a lovers' market, a dance festival and a vast Kumbh
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh celebrates the big pan-Indian festivals, Diwali, Holi, Navratri, Dussehra, Eid and Mahavir Jayanti, with strong regional colour. Some festivals are its own.

In the tribal west, the weekly markets in the week before Holi become **Bhagoria**, a festival of music, dance and courtship. In Bundelkhand, **Rai** dancing by night is accompanied by drums. In Gwalior, the **Tansen Samaroh** brings classical musicians to the tomb each December. In Khajuraho, a dance festival is held each February in front of the temples.

The biggest of all is the **Simhastha Kumbh** at Ujjain, held every 12 years. The last one, in 2016, drew millions of pilgrims to bathe in the Shipra; the next is due in 2028, and the state has been building roads, bridges and ghats for it since 2024.

spotlights.name: Bhagoria
spotlights.spot_it: Crowds of young people in bright turbans and skirts dancing to big dhol drums and flutes at a village market.
spotlights.story_md: In the seven days before Holi, the weekly haats of the Bhil country turn into festivals. Young men and women dress up, dance to the mandal drum and flute, eat and ride swings. Bhagoria is often described as a market where young people elope: the tradition says a boy offers a girl gulal or paan, and if she accepts they may run away to marry. Many Bhil writers say this is exaggerated and that Bhagoria is primarily a harvest and Holi market. Either way it draws tens of thousands of people, and the state now promotes it as a cultural festival.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-known Adivasi festival in central India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Accept a paan, maybe accept a husband.

spotlights.name: Khajuraho Dance Festival
spotlights.spot_it: Classical dancers performing on an open stage at night with floodlit temples behind them.
spotlights.story_md: Since 1975 the state's culture department has held a week of classical dance in front of the Western Group of temples, featuring Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Manipuri and Mohiniyattam. The festival is a way of linking the sculptures to the living dance traditions they show: many temple figures are dancers in poses still taught. The 2024 edition set a Guinness World Record for the largest Kathak dance, with about 1,484 dancers performing together.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Living dance in front of stone dancers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dancers in front of the dancers carved a thousand years ago.

spotlights.name: Simhastha, Ujjain
spotlights.spot_it: Millions of pilgrims crowding the ghats of the Shipra, with sadhus in procession.
spotlights.story_md: Ujjain hosts one of the four Kumbh Melas, held when Jupiter is in Leo (Simha), hence the name Simhastha. It is the only Kumbh where pilgrims bathe in the **Shipra** rather than the Ganga, Godavari or Sangam. Legend says drops of amrit, the nectar of immortality, fell at four places during the gods' fight over it, Ujjain among them. Akharas of sadhus lead the royal baths. The next Simhastha is expected in spring 2028, and the state is planning for crowds in the tens of crores.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the largest gatherings of people on earth.
spotlights.memory_hook: A drop of nectar, twelve years, and crores of pilgrims.

sections.title: How people live: farms, a clean city and hard numbers
sections.intro_md:
About 72% of the state's people lived in villages in 2011, and farming is still the biggest employer. Madhya Pradesh is India's largest producer of **soybean** and among the top producers of wheat, pulses and garlic. Agriculture's growth in the 2010s was among the fastest in the country.

Yet several measures of well-being remain among the worst in India. The state has long had one of the highest **infant mortality rates**: in the Sample Registration System for 2020 it was 43 deaths per 1,000 live births, the highest of any state, against 28 for India. Child malnutrition is high in tribal districts. Literacy in 2011 was 69.3%, below the national 74%.

Against that are new models. **Indore** turned its waste system around after 2016 and was ranked India's cleanest city seven years in a row. Since 2023 the **Ladli Behna** scheme has paid monthly cash to more than a crore women.

spotlights.name: Indore, the cleanest city
spotlights.spot_it: Garbage vans playing a jingle at every door each morning, and six-way segregation bins.
spotlights.story_md: In 2016 Indore was an ordinary, messy Indian city. The municipal corporation removed street bins, sent vehicles door to door playing a catchy song, and made households separate waste into wet, dry and more categories. It cleared an old dump of about 13 lakh tonnes of waste and set up a bio-CNG plant that runs city buses on gas from food waste. Indore was ranked India's cleanest city in the Swachh Survekshan every year from 2017 to 2023. In 2024-25 it was moved into a new 'Super Swachh League' for repeat winners.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that an Indian city can change its habits in a few years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city that sings to its garbage trucks.

spotlights.name: The soybean state
spotlights.spot_it: Green fields of bushy, knee-high plants in the monsoon, turning yellow-brown by October.
spotlights.story_md: Soybean was barely grown in India until the 1970s. On Malwa's black soil it fitted neatly into the monsoon season before winter wheat, and spread so fast that Madhya Pradesh became known as the **Soya State**. It produces roughly 40 to 45% of India's soybean in most years. The crop powers a large processing industry around Indore, whose soymeal is exported as animal feed. Falling prices and erratic rains have left farmers in debt in bad years, and protests over soybean prices broke out again in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A new crop that reshaped a state in a generation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Malwa's black soil grew a 'yellow gold'.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Many of India's most famous figures were born or worked here. Freedom fighters: **Chandra Shekhar Azad**, born in Bhabhra in Alirajpur district, and Tatya Tope, who fought across the state. Rulers: Rani Durgavati of Garha-Mandla, who fought Akbar's army in 1564; Ahilyabai Holkar; the Begums of Bhopal.

Politicians: **Atal Bihari Vajpayee**, three-time Prime Minister, was born in Gwalior. President **Shankar Dayal Sharma** was born in Bhopal. Arjun Singh, Digvijaya Singh and Shivraj Singh Chouhan, the longest-serving chief minister (about 16 years), are all from the state.

Artists: Tansen, Lata Mangeshkar, Kishore Kumar, the poet **Makhanlal Chaturvedi**, the satirist Harishankar Parsai of Jabalpur, the painter **S. H. Raza**, born in Mandla district, and the actor Jaya Bachchan of Jabalpur. The archaeologist V. S. Wakankar of Ujjain found Bhimbetka.

spotlights.name: Chandra Shekhar Azad
spotlights.spot_it: A young man with a twirled moustache, bare-chested, hand on the moustache, in a famous photograph.
spotlights.story_md: Born Chandra Shekhar Tiwari in Bhabhra, a village now renamed after him, he grew up among Bhils and learned to shoot. Arrested at 15 during the Non-cooperation Movement, he told the magistrate his name was 'Azad' (free), his father's 'Swatantrata' (independence) and his home 'jail'. He led the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, with Bhagat Singh. Cornered by police at Alfred Park, Allahabad, on 27 February 1931, he shot himself with his last bullet, keeping his vow never to be taken alive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the most celebrated revolutionaries of the freedom movement.
spotlights.memory_hook: He named himself Free, and died free.

spotlights.name: Atal Bihari Vajpayee
spotlights.spot_it: A white-haired man in a dhoti-kurta, pausing mid-speech with closed eyes.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Gwalior on 25 December 1924, the son of a schoolteacher, Vajpayee studied at Victoria College (now Maharani Laxmi Bai College) in the city. He was a Hindi poet as well as a politician, and became Prime Minister three times: for 13 days in 1996, then 1998 to 2004. His governments carried out the Pokhran-II nuclear tests in 1998 and launched the Golden Quadrilateral highways. He received the Bharat Ratna in 2015. His birthday is marked as Good Governance Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first non-Congress prime minister to complete a full term.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Gwalior poet who held the bomb and the pen.

spotlights.name: Rani Durgavati
spotlights.spot_it: A queen riding a war elephant into battle, in statues and paintings across Jabalpur.
spotlights.story_md: Born a Chandela princess, Durgavati married into the Gond royal family of Garha-Mandla and ruled after her husband died. She defeated Baz Bahadur of Malwa. In 1564 Akbar's general Asaf Khan invaded. She fought from an elephant at Narai near Jabalpur, was wounded by arrows and, rather than be captured, killed herself on 24 June 1564. Jabalpur's university is named after her, and in 2023 a new tiger reserve, Veerangana Durgavati, was created in her name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Gond queen who fought the Mughal empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen on an elephant who chose death over surrender.

sections.title: How it earns: soybean, diamonds and copper
sections.intro_md:
Madhya Pradesh's economy is still built on land. Agriculture and allied activities make up roughly 40 to 45% of the state's output, one of the highest shares in India, against about 18% nationally. The state's GSDP for 2026-27 is projected at about ₹18.5 lakh crore. Its per capita income, around ₹2.17 lakh, is still below the national average.

Under the land lie minerals. Madhya Pradesh has India's only working diamond mine, at **Panna**, one of the largest copper mines at **Malanjkhand**, and large coal fields in Singrauli, called the energy capital of India for its power plants.

Industry clusters around **Indore** and **Pithampur** (autos, pharmaceuticals), Bhopal (heavy electricals, BHEL) and Jabalpur (ordnance factories). Indore is also the state's education hub, with both an IIT and an IIM. Tourism is growing fast around Ujjain's Mahakal Lok, Khajuraho and the tiger parks.

spotlights.name: Panna's diamonds
spotlights.when: Mined for centuries; NMDC mine since 1968
spotlights.spot_it: A shallow pit dug by hand in red gravel, a family sieving and sorting stones on a cloth.
spotlights.story_md: Panna has been famous for diamonds since medieval times. The Majhgawan mine, run by the national NMDC, was India's only mechanised diamond mine, though production has been halted at times for environmental clearance. Around Panna, the government also leases small plots, about 8 by 8 metres, to anyone for a few hundred rupees. People dig by hand, and must deposit what they find at the government diamond office, which auctions them and returns the money minus royalty. Every year a few lucky labourers find stones of several carats and make headlines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Diamond prospecting by lottery, still open to the public.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rent a patch of earth, find a diamond, become news.

sections.title: What is happening now (2024 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The state has been governed by the BJP for most of the last two decades. **Mohan Yadav**, an MLA from Ujjain, became chief minister in December 2023, succeeding Shivraj Singh Chouhan.

The biggest current projects are about cities and water. Indore's metro opened its first stretch on 31 May 2025, timed for Ahilyabai Holkar's 300th birth anniversary, and Bhopal's first metro line opened in December 2025. The **Ken-Betwa river link**, India's first big river-interlinking project, had its foundation stone laid at Khajuraho in December 2024; it will flood part of Panna Tiger Reserve, which conservationists oppose.

In 2025 the toxic waste that had lain at the Union Carbide site in Bhopal for 40 years was moved to Pithampur near Indore and incinerated, amid protests from residents there. Ujjain is building for the **Simhastha of 2028**. And Project Cheetah has expanded from Kuno to Gandhi Sagar sanctuary.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
A few stories about Madhya Pradesh are repeated so often that they feel true. Here is how they hold up.

**'Khajuraho is an erotic temple complex.'** Mostly false. The erotic panels are famous but form a small share, around a tenth, of the sculpture. The temples are dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and the Jain tirthankaras.

**'The old Parliament House was copied from the Mitaoli temple.'** Unproven. The resemblance is real; no document from Lutyens or Baker says so.

**'Tansen could light lamps by singing.'** Legend. The story of raga Deepak is centuries old but there is no historical account.

**'Mowgli was a real wolf boy from Seoni.'** Partly. Kipling set the stories in the Seoni hills from books and reports. A real 'wolf child' was reported from Seoni in the 1830s, but there is no evidence it inspired him directly.

**'Bhopal's gas disaster is over.'** False. Contaminated groundwater and chronic illness persist in neighbourhoods around the old plant.

**'Madhya Pradesh is the geographic centre of India.'** Roughly true: the centre of the country's mainland, by most calculations, falls in the state, though different methods give different spots.

sections.title: Recap: Madhya Pradesh in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. India's second-largest state, at the centre of the country, formed 1 November 1956; Chhattisgarh split off in 2000.
2. Bhimbetka: 750 rock shelters, painted from around 10,000 BCE; found by Wakankar in 1957.
3. Sanchi, the Heliodorus pillar and Udayagiri: early Buddhism, early Krishna worship and Gupta art.
4. Gwalior's Chaturbhuj temple has the oldest stone zero (876 CE); Khajuraho's temples date to about 950 to 1050.
5. Ahilyabai Holkar and the Begums of Bhopal: a century of women rulers.
6. Most tigers of any state (785), Kanha's barasingha, Chambal's gharials and Kuno's cheetahs.
7. India's largest tribal population: Bhils, Gonds, Baiga; Gond and Bhil art.
8. Tansen, the Gwalior gharana, Maihar, Lata and Kishore.
9. Chanderi and Maheshwari saris; poha-jalebi and Sarafa at midnight.
10. Hard truths: the Bhopal gas disaster, high infant mortality; new ones: Indore's clean streets and metros.

best_facts.fact: The oldest known zero carved in stone, a small circle in the numbers 270 and 50, is in a Vishnu shrine at Gwalior Fort, dated 876 CE.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 0 on every keyboard has a stone ancestor in a Gwalior garden grant.

best_facts.fact: Bhimbetka was brought to light in 1957 by an archaeologist who, by his own account, noticed its rocks from a passing train.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the world's great prehistoric art sites was found through a train window.

best_facts.fact: From 1819 to 1926 the state of Bhopal was ruled by four women in a row, one of whom governed wearing a burqa and became the first chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University.
best_facts.why_surprising: A century of queens in a conservative princely state.

best_facts.fact: A Greek ambassador named Heliodorus raised a pillar at Vidisha around 113 BCE declaring himself a devotee of Vasudeva (Krishna).
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the earliest records of Krishna worship was left by a Greek.

best_facts.fact: Madhya Pradesh has 785 wild tigers (2022 estimate), more than any other state and over a fifth of India's total.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most tigers live not in the Sundarbans or the Himalaya but in the middle of India.

best_facts.fact: Most white tigers in the world's zoos descend from one cub, Mohan, caught near Rewa in 1951.
best_facts.why_surprising: A global zoo phenomenon goes back to a single animal from Madhya Pradesh.

best_facts.fact: At Orchha, Rama is worshipped as the reigning king and receives a daily guard of honour from the state police.
best_facts.why_surprising: A god with a police salute.

best_facts.fact: The supercontinent Gondwana is named, via Indian geology, after the land of the Gond people.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tribe's name stretches across 300 million years of Earth history.

best_facts.fact: Arrested at 15, Chandra Shekhar Azad told a magistrate his name was 'Free', his father's 'Independence' and his address 'Jail'.
best_facts.why_surprising: A teenager's courtroom joke became a national legend.

best_facts.fact: In Panna, anyone can lease a small plot to dig for diamonds and must hand finds to a government diamond office for auction.
best_facts.why_surprising: A public diamond lottery still runs in modern India.

best_facts.fact: The Narmada skull cap found at Hathnora in 1982 is still the only ancient human skull fossil ever found in India.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole country's fossil record of early humans rests largely on one find.

best_facts.fact: Kanha's hard-ground barasingha fell to about 66 animals in 1970 and has recovered to around a thousand.
best_facts.why_surprising: A near-extinct deer brought back by a single park.

best_facts.fact: On Sanchi's carved gateways the Buddha never appears in human form, only as a throne, a tree, footprints or a wheel.
best_facts.why_surprising: The central figure is absent from every scene.

best_facts.fact: In Indore's Sarafa Bazaar, jewellers close at night and food stalls take over the same street until 2 or 3 am.
best_facts.why_surprising: A jewellery market turns into a midnight food street every day.

best_facts.fact: The Kadaknath chicken of Jhabua is black inside and out, including its meat and organs.
best_facts.why_surprising: A black chicken, down to the bone.

best_facts.fact: Kuno was prepared for Gir lions that never came; it got African cheetahs instead in 2022.
best_facts.why_surprising: The park waited for lions and got cheetahs.

best_facts.fact: Indore was ranked India's cleanest city every year from 2017 to 2023, after a reform that began in 2016.
best_facts.why_surprising: A city changed its reputation in a single year.

best_facts.fact: Jai Vilas Palace's chandeliers are each said to weigh about 3.5 tonnes; the story goes that elephants were hauled onto the roof to test it.

side_dish.title: How zero travelled from Gwalior to your phone
side_dish.body_md:
The circle carved at Gwalior in 876 CE was not the first idea of zero. Babylonians used a placeholder sign, and the Maya had a zero glyph. What Indian mathematicians added was zero as a **number** you can calculate with, inside a **place-value** system of ten digits.

In 628 CE the astronomer **Brahmagupta**, working at Bhinmal in Rajasthan, wrote rules for it: a number minus itself is zero; zero times anything is zero. He even tried to define division by zero, and got it wrong in a way mathematicians still argue about.

The Sanskrit word was **shunya**, empty. Arab scholars in Baghdad translated Indian astronomy in the 8th century and called it **sifr**. In the 1200s the Italian Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, learned the 'Indian figures' in North Africa and wrote a book telling European merchants to use them. Sifr became Latin **zephirum**, then Italian **zero**. The same root gave English the word **cipher**.

Europe resisted for centuries. In 1299 Florence banned the new numerals in official accounts, partly because a 0 could easily be changed into a 6 or a 9. Roman numerals have no zero at all, which is why there was no year 0 between 1 BCE and 1 CE.

Next time you type 0, remember that the oldest one carved in stone is still on a temple wall in Gwalior, counting 50 garlands of flowers a day.

offline_task.title: Make Indori poha for breakfast
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. 20 minutes.**

- 1.5 cups thick poha (flattened rice)
- 1 small onion, finely chopped
- 1 green chilli, chopped
- 1 teaspoon mustard seeds, 1 teaspoon fennel seeds (saunf), a pinch of hing
- Half a teaspoon turmeric, 1 teaspoon sugar, salt
- 1 tablespoon oil, lemon, fresh coriander
- To top: a handful of sev (thin besan noodles), raw onion, pomegranate seeds, and chaat masala if you have no jeeravan

**Steps**
1. Rinse the poha in a sieve under running water for 10 seconds. Do not soak it. Let it sit 5 minutes to soften. Mix in turmeric, sugar and salt.
2. Heat oil, add mustard seeds; when they crackle add fennel, hing, chilli and onion. Cook until the onion is soft, not brown.
3. Add the poha, mix gently, cover and keep on the lowest heat for 3 to 4 minutes. In Indore it is often steamed over a pot of boiling water instead.
4. Squeeze lemon over, add coriander, and pile sev, raw onion and pomegranate on top just before eating.

If you can buy or fry jalebi, eat a piece in between spoonfuls. That sweet and salty swing is the whole point.
